parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
During the transmission of a signal, attenuation occurs and noise is picked up.

State what is meant by:
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the size of the signal as it travels a long distance along a wire or fibre - does it stay the same height on an oscilloscope trace?
parts.proper_answer: Attenuation is the loss of signal power (amplitude or intensity) as the signal passes through the transmission line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the journey**
Think of sending a loud sound down a long corridor. By the far end it is quieter. In the same way, as an electrical or optical signal travels, some of its energy is absorbed or scattered by the wire, fibre or free space.

Step 2: **State the definition**
So attenuation means the progressive decrease in the power, amplitude or intensity of the transmitted signal. It is why amplifiers or repeaters are needed for long-distance transmission.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about listening to a radio with crackle and hiss in the background - where does that extra sound come from?
Hint 2: Think about how this extra disturbance combines with the wanted signal as they travel together.
parts.proper_answer: Noise is an unwanted, random signal that is superposed (added) onto the transmitted signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Unwanted and random**
Noise is not part of your message. It comes from outside sources like thermal motion of electrons, lightning, nearby motors or crosstalk from other cables. It is random - you cannot predict its exact shape.

Step 2: **Added to your signal**
As the wanted signal travels, this random disturbance adds itself on top of it, so $$V_{received} = V_{signal} + V_{noise}$$ The receiver then gets a distorted version of the original shape.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: By reference to (a)(ii), explain the advantage of the transmission of the signal in digital form rather than in analogue form.

markscheme_points.text: noise can be eliminated (from digital signals) or signal can be regenerated (from digital signals)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the difference between copying an exact wavy shape with all its fuzz, and just deciding if a pulse is a 0 or a 1 even if it looks a bit fuzzy.
parts.proper_answer: For a digital signal the original 0 or 1 levels can be recognised and a clean new signal regenerated, so noise can be eliminated.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why analogue suffers**
With an analogue signal every tiny change in voltage matters, so once noise is added you cannot separate noise from signal. Amplifying it amplifies the noise too.

Step 2: **Why digital wins**
With a digital signal only two states matter, high and low. Even if noise makes a 1 a little smaller or a 0 a little bigger, the repeater can still decide correctly that it was meant to be 1 or 0 and then transmit a fresh, clean pulse. The noise does not build up.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Part of an analogue signal is shown in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

The signal is to be transmitted in digital form.

The analogue signal is sampled at a frequency of $1.0 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$ using an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). The ADC produces 4-bit numbers.

The times $t$ at which the analogue signal is sampled are shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2

On Fig. 4.2:
parts.text: for the digital number at time $t = 3.0\text{ ms}$, underline the least significant bit (LSB)
hints: Hint 1: Think of ordinary decimal numbers - which digit changes the value least if you change it, the left-most or the right-most?
parts.proper_answer: 010$\underline{1}$ - the right-most bit (the $1$-valued bit) is the LSB.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **MSB versus LSB**
In a 4-bit number the bits from left to right have values $8, 4, 2, 1$. The Most Significant Bit (MSB) on the left changes the value by 8, the Least Significant Bit (LSB) on the right changes it by only 1.

Step 2: **Apply to 0101**
For $$0101 = 0\times 8 + 1\times 4 + 0\times 2 + 1\times 1 = 5$$ the final $1$ on the right is the $1$s place, so underline that last digit.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: state the digital numbers corresponding to the sampling times between time $t = 4.0\text{ ms}$ and time $t = 6.0\text{ ms}$.

markscheme_points.text: 0110 at t = 5.0 ms and 0100 at t = 6.0 ms

hints: Hint 1: Read the signal voltage in mV from Fig. 4.1 at $t = 4.0$, $5.0$ and $6.0$ ms and compare with the voltages already given for $t = 0$ to $3.0$ ms.
Hint 2: Notice the pattern so far: $2\text{ mV}$ gives $0010 = 2$, $6\text{ mV}$ gives $0110 = 6$ - so what binary numbers will the new voltages correspond to?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Calibrate from given data**
Look at Fig. 4.2. At $t=0$, $V \approx 2.0\text{ mV}$ gives $0010 = 2$ in decimal. At $t=1.0\text{ ms}$, $V \approx 6.0\text{ mV}$ gives $0110 = 6$. At $t=2.0\text{ ms}$, $V \approx 4.0\text{ mV}$ gives $0100 = 4$. So $1\text{ mV}$ corresponds to 1 ADC level.

Step 2: **Read new voltages**
From Fig. 4.1: at $t = 4.0\text{ ms}$, $V \approx 8\text{ mV}$; at $t = 5.0\text{ ms}$, $V \approx 6$ to $7\text{ mV}$ nearest to $6\text{ mV}$; at $t = 6.0\text{ ms}$, $V \approx 4$ to $5\text{ mV}$ nearest to $4\text{ mV}$.

Step 3: **Convert to 4-bit binary**
$$8 = 1\times 8 + 0\times 4 + 0\times 2 + 0\times 1 = 1000$$ $$6 = 0\times 8 + 1\times 4 + 1\times 2 + 0\times 1 = 0110$$ $$4 = 0\times 8 + 1\times 4 + 0\times 2 + 0\times 1 = 0100$$

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem: The transmitted digital signal is converted back to an analogue signal using a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC).

markscheme_points.text: series of equally-spaced steps of width 1 ms
each step in correct time interval (0–1 ms, 1–2 etc.)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what a DAC does between samples - does it follow the smooth curve or hold the last digital value steady until the next sample arrives?
Hint 2: Work out the sampling interval from the $1.0 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$ sampling frequency and use it as the width of each flat step.
Hint 3: Convert the first four digital numbers 0010, 0110, 0100, 0101 to decimal to get the heights of the steps from $t = 0$ to $4.0$ ms.
parts.proper_answer: Staircase of flat steps of width $1.0\text{ ms}$: level 2 from 0-1 ms, level 6 from 1-2 ms, level 4 from 2-3 ms, level 5 from 3-4 ms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Hold that value**
A DAC does not recreate the smooth original. It outputs a constant voltage level equal to the last received digital number, then jumps suddenly when the next number arrives. This gives a staircase shape.

Step 2: **Find the step width**
Sampling frequency $$f = 1.0 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$$ so period $$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{1.0 \times 10^3} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 1.0\text{ ms}$$ Each level therefore lasts $1.0\text{ ms}$: 0 to 1 ms, 1 to 2 ms, 2 to 3 ms, 3 to 4 ms.

Step 3: **Find the step heights**
Convert binary to decimal output level: $$0010 = 2$$ $$0110 = 6$$ $$0100 = 4$$ $$0101 = 5$$ So draw a horizontal line at 2 from $t=0$ to $1\text{ ms}$, jump to 6 from $1$ to $2\text{ ms}$, drop to 4 from $2$ to $3\text{ ms}$, rise to 5 from $3$ to $4\text{ ms}$, with vertical jumps at the sampling times.
